own_scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix
own_scenes.desc: La historia de Hendrix se ha escrito desde el rock (blanco) y no desde el funk (negro), pese a su herencia, su formación y sus bandas negras. Criado en el Seattle multirracial, en el ejército descubrió el blues de Nashville y el sonido de Memphis, tocó con Little Richard, aprendió de Albert King y fue guitarrista de los Isley Brothers en Harlem, protegido por la red social negra. Chas Chandler lo llevó a Londres; en Monterey (1967) nació una nueva era. «If 6 Was 9» («voy a ondear mi bandera de bicho raro») articulaba los choques culturales que él provocaba. En Woodstock tocó con una banda multirracial de seis músicos con percusionistas afrolatinos que el ingeniero borró de la mezcla; luego formó la Band of Gypsys con Buddy Miles y Billy Cox, grabó con Lightnin’ Rod de los Last Poets y quiso tocar para los Panteras. Murió en 1970, un día después de tocar con War. No tuvo música de baile ni sitio en la radio negra, pero su huella en Miles, Prince, Bootsy, Clinton, Eddie Hazel, los Isley o Stevie Wonder fue profunda.

refs.q: The legacy of Jimi Hendrix has been completely misunderstood.
refs.para: The legacy of Jimi Hendrix has been completely misunderstood. Hendrix was and continues to be a part of the rock tradition of music (which really means “white” tradition), despite his black American heritage, his black American musical training, and his work in all-black bands. And while his life as a black musician was central to his identity and his legacy, most rock histories discuss Hendrix exclusively in terms of rock.
refs.chapter: Cap. 9: Black rock: Givin’ It Back

refs.q: Jimi’s African ensemble, exposed to the world, vanished with a sweep of the mixing board.
refs.para: Jimi’s African ensemble, exposed to the world, vanished with a sweep of the mixing board. As biographer Dave Henderson wrote, “The sound the African drums made was lost, an entire acoustical realm lost in the air.” This may be a small point, but careers are made at significant points in history, as James Brown’s was solidified after Dr. King’s death. The best-selling Woodstock soundtrack featured only “Purple Haze” and Jimi’s solo performance of “The Star Spangled Banner,” the subtleties of which, the ironies of which—the knowledge of which—evaded the typical black listener, who was not even exposed to Hendrix on black radio. While the ultimate concert was a showcase for the propulsive Latin rock of the then-unknown act Santana, and Sly Stone’s triumphant rendition of “Higher” is legendary, Jimi’s efforts to flow musically in that same direction were sadly missed.
refs.chapter: Cap. 9: Black rock: Givin’ It Back

refs.q: Jimi was as much a part of black music as any artist who ever lived.
refs.para: Musicians from all walks of life came to his funeral, but his image remained: He was a rock star, and died that way. The passage of time has not helped. The essential musical connections that were reflected deeply by other artists like Miles Davis, Prince, Bootsy Collins, George Clinton, Norman Whitfield, Ernie Isley, Eddie Hazel, Stevie Wonder, and Marvin Gaye were apparently missed by the music establishment. Jimi was as much a part of black music as any artist who ever lived. But his history has been written from a rock (read: white) perspective, not a funk (read: black) perspective. The true story of Jimi Hendrix as a black musician has been obfuscated, and twisted by myth like the black roots of the Egyptians.

own_scenes.desc: Intérprete de la tradición del blues eléctrico que ya había incorporado buena parte del estilo psicodélico, incluido su gusto por lo visual. Murió antes de que el heavy fuese un género definido, pero influyó enormemente en su música y su puesta en escena por su carisma y su talento, y porque encarnaba a la vez las dos tradiciones sobre las que se levanta el género. Con Cream introduce en el blues rock elementos del jazz, sobre todo los solos instrumentales extensos.

notes.chapter: Cap. 3: Hacer la música: los dioses del metal
notes.text: Pese a la influencia reconocida de Hendrix, hasta finales de los ochenta casi no hubo músicos negros en el heavy (Phil Lynott, de Thin Lizzy, es una de las pocas excepciones): nacido en ciudades industriales inglesas y llegado a Estados Unidos en plena autosegregación cultural negra tras 1968, el heavy se convirtió en el «blues de los chicos blancos». Al propio Hendrix lo criticaron otros negros por tocar música «blanca».

refs.q: He died before heavy metal became a well-defined genre, but he exerted an enormous influence on the eventual emergence of heavy metal
refs.para: Heavy metal added psychedelic/acid-rock music to the basic structure of blues rock.¹² Hendrix was already on to much of the psychedelic style, including its focus on visuals. He died before heavy metal became a well-defined genre, but he exerted an enormous influence on the eventual emergence of heavy metal through his personal charisma and talent, and through his embodiment of the two major traditions that formed the foundation for the genre. Psychedelic music was noted for its mysterious, drug-trip lyrics, and for the colorful clothes and lighting that marked its performances. Musically, it is jazzlike, but with a distinctive repetition of simple phrases. Using few and simple chords, it creates a very complex whole. Like nineteenth-century romantic tone poems, such as Smetana’s “The Moldau,” which aim at re-creating an object musically, acid rock tries to re-create an LSD experience. Acid rock was aimed not at one’s legs or crotch, but at one’s head. It wasn’t dance music. Getting lost in the music was “getting” the music. This ecstatic use of music was taken up by heavy metal in a Diony-sian key, for heavy metal revels in the powers of life.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: But historical circumstance made heavy metal the “white-boy blues.”
refs.para: Heavy metal is a preserve not only of the youthful and the physically well endowed but also of white males. The genre is widely acknowledged by fans and artists to have been heavily influenced by a black artist, Jimi Hendrix. But until the late 1980s there were almost no black heavy metal musicians. (Exceptions such as the late Phil Lynott of Thin Lizzy can be counted on the fingers of one hand.) The image of the heavy metal star as a hypermacho, athletic, strong, lustful, and musically competent individual certainly corresponds with white stereotypes of the black male in the West. Indeed, Hendrix (dis)played these characteristics to the hilt. But historical circumstance made heavy metal the “white-boy blues.”

scenes.name: Llega la psicodelia británica
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 la palabra «psychedelic» llegó a Gran Bretaña: el Melody Maker la presentó el 22 de octubre como «el gran contraataque americano» y la prensa la aplicó a los Move, Creation, los Who y los californianos Misunderstood («vamos de viaje al subconsciente»): freak-outs, volumen y asalto sonoro. Fue el momento en que empezó el rock: virtuosismo, improvisación y ambición, aún contenidos en el single. Cream, tres veteranos del R&B, sacó «I Feel Free»; Jimi Hendrix, llegado en septiembre con Chas Chandler, era el negro americano empapado de soul, blues, Dylan y ácido que los británicos imitaban: «Hey Joe» y «Stone Free» («Free Feeling»). Donovan volvió con «Sunshine Superman». El 23 de diciembre abrió UFO en el Blarney Club, la primera noche del underground, con Pink Floyd en improvisaciones de diez minutos; en Nochevieja, Psychedelicamania en el Roundhouse con los Move, Pink Floyd y los Who. Los mods quedaban atrás.

scenes.name: Contracultura, Sgt. Pepper y Woodstock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.

scenes.name: Psicodelia y acid-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En 1965 San Francisco se convierte en la ciudad más efervescente del país: los Grateful Dead tocan en los «acid tests» de Ken Kesey, nace la escena hippy y en 1966-67 llega el verano del amor. El acid-rock, evolución del folk-rock pensada como banda sonora del viaje de LSD, es el equivalente rockero de la pintura abstracta, el free jazz y la poesía beat: su gran invento es la «jam», con la guitarra eléctrica al mando y un espíritu zen en lugar del dolor del blues. Jefferson Airplane encarnan la era; los Grateful Dead inventan la improvisación colectiva libre (Anthem Of The Sun, Live Dead); Kaleidoscope, Moby Grape, Quicksilver, Blue Cheer o Fifty Foot Hose amplían el abanico. Monterey y Sgt Pepper (1967) convierten lo alternativo en mainstream. Fuera de California, Jimi Hendrix declara la guerra a la armonía occidental con su guitarra.

podcast.title: Early Adopter of Wah-Wah Pedal
podcast.body: Jimmy Hendrix, an "up and coming guitarist," was one of the two customers convinced by Henry Goldrich to buy a wah-wah pedal at Manie's Music in the mid-1960s. This purchase significantly changed his playing style and, by extension, the direction of guitar-based rock and roll. "One was up and coming guitarist named Jimmy Hendrix. xref.title: Performing During Woodstock 99 Fires (1999)
xref.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers took the stage at Woodstock 99 on Sunday night amidst a growing mob mentality and escalating violence. A peace group had distributed 100,000 candles for a vigil during their set, but the unruly crowd used these candles to set fires, looting vendor booths, burning plywood walls, and even toppling a speaker tower. The situation was further exacerbated when the band launched into their cover of Jimi Hendrix's "Fire," which seemingly encouraged more arson. "it was probably a really bad idea for the chili peppers to launch into their cover of Jimmy Hendrix's fire, which of course only encouraged more fire."

xref.title: Tommy Ramone's Early Career and Production Role
xref.body: Tommy Erdelyi (Tommy Ramone) escaped communism as a child, fleeing Hungary with his parents to New York. He was a skilled guitarist and, significantly, worked as a recording engineer at The Record Plant, where he notably worked with Jimi Hendrix. This experience led him to produce the Ramones' first three albums, and later co-produced their fourth and eighth albums. "Not only did he play guitar, but he also found a very sweet gig working as a recording engineer in a studio called the Record Plant. One of the very first people he got to work for was Jimmy Hendricks."
